course_information.title: Paint Sales & Customer Consultation
course_information.description: Guide a customer from a paint project question to a practical product-and-supplies plan.
course_information.scope: General independent hardware retail; not store-specific
course_information.restrictions: Retail product consultation only. No licensed trade, lead remediation, mold remediation, or hazardous-material handling instruction.
learning_objectives: Use discovery questions to understand a paint project.
Explain coverage estimates without guaranteeing quantities.
Compare products using relevant label-backed benefits.
Recommend a complete but appropriate project supply list.
Confirm next steps and escalate technical uncertainties.

lessons.title: Discover the Project Before the Product
lessons.objective: Lead a useful paint conversation with project questions.
lessons.why_this_matters: The customer may ask for a specific product before describing the actual job.

content.heading: Begin with the surface
content.text: Ask what is being painted, whether it is new or previously coated, and whether it is indoors or outdoors.

content.heading: Understand the result
content.text: Ask what matters most: appearance, cleaning, exposure, timing, or budget. Do not assume the most expensive option is best.

content.heading: Confirm constraints
content.text: Find out whether the customer has tools, how soon the area must be used, and whether there are damaged or damp surfaces.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A customer requests “bathroom paint.” You learn the issue is recurring moisture and peeling. You avoid promising paint alone will fix the cause.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Ask: “What is happening on the wall now, and has the moisture problem been addressed?”
lessons.common_mistakes: Starting with price; recommending a coating before asking about surface condition.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Refer unresolved moisture, suspected mold, or unknown previous coatings to appropriate help.

unscored_practice.question: Which question is the strongest opening?

choices.text: How much do you want to spend?
What surface are you painting and what is on it now?
Would you like our most expensive paint?

unscored_practice.explanation: The surface and current condition determine the useful next questions.

lessons.title: Estimate Paint Quantities Responsibly
lessons.objective: Explain how to estimate coverage and why actual use varies.
lessons.why_this_matters: Too little paint delays a project. Too much may create unnecessary expense.

content.heading: Measure the area
content.text: For a rectangular wall, multiply width by height to estimate square footage. Add wall areas for the full project. Openings can be accounted for when practical.

content.heading: Check product coverage
content.text: Use the coverage range printed on the chosen product or its official calculator. Surface texture, porosity, application method, and number of coats affect the result.

content.heading: Explain the estimate
content.text: A coverage figure is an estimate, not a promise. Round purchases based on available container sizes and the customer’s project needs.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A customer has two walls measuring 10 feet wide by 8 feet high. You calculate 160 square feet before considering doors, windows, and coats. You then check the selected product’s coverage.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Say: “This is the wall area. Let’s check this paint’s stated coverage and the number of coats your project needs.”
lessons.common_mistakes: Using one universal coverage rate; forgetting multiple coats; guaranteeing the estimate.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Ask a specialist for unusual textures, spray application, or large commercial estimates.

unscored_practice.question: Two 10-by-8-foot walls have what combined area before openings?
unscored_practice.explanation: Each wall is 10 × 8 = 80 square feet. Two walls total 160 square feet.

lessons.title: Compare Paint Options Without Pressure
lessons.objective: Use customer priorities and verified claims to compare choices.
lessons.why_this_matters: Customers benefit from a clear explanation of value, not a sales pitch.

content.heading: Compare relevant features
content.text: Review intended use, sheen options, preparation requirements, coverage, and manufacturer-stated performance.

content.heading: Explain price in context
content.text: A lower shelf price may not reflect the full project cost if preparation or extra coats differ. Do not promise fewer coats unless the specific product supports that claim.

content.heading: Offer a choice
content.text: Present two appropriate options and explain a meaningful difference. Let the customer decide.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A customer is repainting a high-traffic hallway. You compare two suitable wall paints using their published cleaning guidance and prices.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Say: “Both are labeled for interior walls. This one has a different cleaning claim. Would you like to compare the label details?”
lessons.common_mistakes: Calling one product “best” without context; inventing durability claims.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Escalate warranty, special-use, and performance claims you cannot verify.

unscored_practice.question: What makes a responsible product comparison?

choices.text: A claim that expensive paint is always better
A comparison based on customer needs and verified product information
A promise of no future touch-ups
A guarantee that one coat always works

unscored_practice.explanation: Use the customer’s project and the selected products’ documented claims.

lessons.title: Build the Right Supply List
lessons.objective: Identify needed preparation, application, and cleanup items.
lessons.why_this_matters: A good sale helps the customer complete the project without avoidable return trips.

content.heading: Think through the steps
content.text: Consider cleaning, repairs, masking, protecting nearby surfaces, priming if needed, applying, and cleaning up.

content.heading: Match tools to the task
content.text: Brushes, rollers, trays, extension poles, drop cloths, tape, and abrasives vary by job. Use the coating label for compatible applicators.

content.heading: Recommend, do not bundle blindly
content.text: Explain why each item may be useful. Check what the customer already owns.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A customer buys paint for a small bedroom and already owns a roller frame. You ask whether they have the right cover, a tray, a brush for edges, and surface protection.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Say: “What tools do you already have? We can fill in only what is missing.”
lessons.common_mistakes: Adding unrelated items; forgetting cleanup or surface protection.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Ask for help with specialty coatings, spray equipment, or respiratory protection requirements.

unscored_practice.question: What is the best way to recommend add-on supplies?

choices.text: Include every accessory in the department
Ask what the customer has and explain supplies needed for the steps

lessons.title: Close with a Project Recap
lessons.objective: Confirm the plan and help the customer leave prepared.
lessons.why_this_matters: A clear final recap reduces confusion after the customer gets home.

content.heading: Repeat the plan
content.text: Summarize the surface, selected product, estimated quantity, key preparation, and application guidance.

content.heading: Point to trusted instructions
content.text: Show the label or official technical guidance for timing, ventilation, and cleanup. Do not replace those instructions with guesses.

content.heading: Invite follow-up
content.text: Tell the customer how to get more help if an unexpected condition appears before application.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A customer chooses paint for a previously painted door. You recap cleaning, checking for damage, label-based prep, and appropriate application tools.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Say: “Before you go, here is what we selected and what the label says to do first.”
lessons.common_mistakes: Ending immediately after payment; promising a specific finish result.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Escalate if the customer describes bubbling, widespread peeling, or unexplained dampness.

completion_content.lifetime_points_rule: Award 10 lifetime points for each question answered correctly only once across attempts.
completion_content.trophy_rule: Award one standard trophy upon first pass.
completion_content.replay_rule: After passing, quiz replay for competitions is allowed. Competition points are separate from lifetime points and trophies; lesson review optional.
completion_content.availability_rule: Store availability is controlled by an administrator; publishing does not assign to every store.
completion_content.completion_message: You completed PD-102: Paint Sales & Customer Consultation. Use your project questions and the product label to guide your next customer conversation.
